Being a healthcare professional is hard, especially if you don’t know what to expect. We think hearing from you will help give medical students and new healthcare providers a better idea of what to expect. We’d like you to write a letter to a new healthcare provider who will begin working at a medical facility like yours.



In your letter, please describe what you have shared today about providing healthcare in a way that prioritizes patients’ perspectives and meets them where they are. Try to use examples from your own experiences or examples of things you’ve seen.   



Feel free to draw from these themes discussed today:



	Research suggests that finding concordance in patient and physician goals promotes patient self-efficacy –patients believe that they have the capacity to execute behaviors necessary to improve their health. 
	Small changes in a physician’s practice can vastly improve patient trust in medical care – such as adopting a patient-centered approach in healthcare visits. 
	Sensitivity toward the circumstances that might get in a patient’s way along their journey toward maximized health allows the patient to be active in their healthcare, increasing compliance and long-term well-being.


Don't worry about spelling or grammar; Just try to describe your experiences. We think it will help new healthcare professionals a lot. Please respond with at least three meaningful sentences to share.

column26: It’s important because my way may not be the patient’s way. What I mean by that is my way of care can be different than the quality or type of care a patient expects or is accustomed to. column64:
It is of the utmost importance that you look at and treat your patient as a family member or as someone looking into the mirror. Yes, YOU. Treat your patients how you expect and want to be treated. 

Learn who they are, not just their diseases or maladies. Learn about what makes them happy and what kind of lifestyle they have. Learn about help they have or may not have. Keep in mind that you are not just a number to your patient, and your patient should never be just a number to you. 

Some patients are easy and malleable. However, there will be times when your patience is tested. Good! How you treat the patient in these trying times speaks to who you are as a medical professional. You’ll notice that I didn’t say what you are as a medical professional. That’s because you are a human being; not a what, but a who. Treat every patient with that in mind and it will make all the difference.

column75: Technology has worked it's way into most of my life.  My alarm on my phone wakes me up. I then have Alexa turn off thr white noise that helps me sleep.  I then ask Alexa what the weather will be so I know what to wear.  When I go to new places, I rely on Google Maps to keep me from getting lost.  All my communication is done electronically either by call on my cell,  text, email or video.  I research any vacations that I take online looking for the best price and the book it all on line.  Who needs a travel agent anymore.   My music is a streamed or on satellite radio.   I order food delivery from my phone on an app, and if I'm in the city, another app calls me a ride.  Then I monitor my steps, activity,  heart rate,  oxygen saturation,  and sleep patterns on my smart watch.  I'm sure there is more,  but that is enough for now.

Welcome to the rewarding and often complicated world of medicine. 

You will see a myriad of patients with varying levels of medical knowledge. This is where you will deliver possibly the most important service you can provide, in teaching. Learn about your patients, this will help immensely in creating a comprehensive care plan that they will adhere to. Talk to them, not at them. Hear what they have to say. You will be their advocate. Ask yourself daily, how would I treat the person I love the most, what would my plan of care look like? Then execute it as if the person, who you love was seated in front of you.

Invite questions 
Teach, do not lecture
Do not judge
Listen 
Involve family
Offer viable options and small measurable goals
Be encouraging 
Share a personal story, which will help humanize, in a time where patients are scared and/or intimated
Most of all, be empathetic. 

You will see patients from all walks of life. Please treat them with the utmost respect, devoid of judgement. Their very life depends on you. 

Good luck and God speed.

column64: The best health care providers use empowerment and motivational techniques to help share information that is often complicated, scary and hard to follow because of learning difficulties, reading or math difficulties or other psychosocial issues. column64: Nursing is hard work everyday. Nursing is seeing people at their worst and most vulnerable and many of them are so frightened that they will not treat you well.  Many will lash out at out due to their fear, you will initially take this response personally because all you want to do is help.  They are rejecting you and will want to reject them.  But you will find that just as you might comfort a small child, so you will reach out to comfort your patients.  Many times this means just sitting quietly next to them, letting them know that you are there; available.  In your busy work the number of patients that you are assigned will feel overwhelming and it is.  There will not be time to do the kind of job you want to and you will be pulled away from those that need you because there are others that need you too. You will struggle with wanting to do the job you were educated to do and not being able to do it.  The most rewarding parts of nursing are often the same parts that you will not have time to do.  Your job will be filled with required tasks.  As you learn the workflow you will come to find a way to begin to meet these needs but not everyday and not for every patient.  You may want to quit.  But if you do, there will be many less nurses to care for the patients and less time that they will have to meet patients needs.  Do the best you can.  You are a success everyday that you come to work. You are doing the best that you can and will continue to work to improve your skills and help as many patients as you can.  You can reach out to others on the unit and there are also employee assistance persons that can help you to manage the personal stress of the work environment.  Best wishes.

Please understand that you are a team member in the patients life. You are not above them, you are with them. Understand that they put trust in you. It is your responsibility to keep that trust by open communication, understanding them as an individual. If there js question, the patient can clarify.

Each patient has their own history which influences their thoughts. Please listen and acknowledge there is a lot that you don’t know. There is a lot they don’t know. This is why you meet.

I watch doctors treat people the same from patient to patient.. they tend to pass the feelings of the difficult patient onto the next patient. Don’t become desensitized.

Here is an example, I rarely go to the doctor. I went to the express clinic because I could not breath. I was told it was muscle skeletal. He didn’t listen. And to add, assessment documented did not happen.

Tuesday I called my regular doctor and got in Wednesday am. He didn’t listen. He called me anxiety. He sent me chiropractor later that day. At this time, I was defeated.

Back to the chiropractor on Friday. He listened and understood. He sent me back to a different doctor and through testing, I was diagnosed with bilateral pulmonary embolism that were extremely close to irreversible damage.

It took 2 desensitized providers to get me to the chiropractor that listened. The chiropractor listened and trusted. He sent me to a provider he knew would listen. There was zero reason for me to be called anxiety. I don’t go to the doctor. I didn’t create their minimization and desensitization. They CHOSE to pass that along. And being a nurse, I lost trust. The minimization caused by desensitization nearly caused my life. 

To new doctors- patients come in as individuals. They don’t come as a whole group of your past challenging patients. Hear your patients and listen to your patients. If for no other reason, do it because it’s your job. Yes, you are in an elite field. Yes, you make the calls. But also know, yes, you can make errors. When the patient (like myself) link errors to simple communication, the error becomes more. 

As a nurse and as a patient, I will not trust the early providers. Not because they made an error but because prior to the error, they didn’t see me as a person. The damage in relationship can’t be replaced

Dear person my age,
Using technology for entertainment became even more necessary because of the restrictions placed on citizens during the COVID-19 pandemic. People needed to have something to do to take their minds off of the deaths and tragedy’s happening around them. Suicide and depression due to loneliness and stress from a loss of a job,  was part of the many factors that led to people’s death during a time when death was happening due to the pandemic. Hospital stays were longer due to COVID-19. As a healthcare provider, watching a patient lose hope during their battle with COVID because they could not have family visit them for their entire hospital stay to keep their spirits up was truly heartbreaking. Healthcare providers definitely had to innovate during this time and use any method they had to bring these patients family’s to them with out breaking restrictions.

column64: Thank you for joining this truly fulfilling yet challenging field. We need more HCPs who are easy to talk to, personable, caring, empathic, kind and professional. There will be days you question why you became a HCP. Think about what your “why” is. What drove you to this field? Try to remember this during shifts when you feel burnt out, discouraged, experience compassion fatigue. And please please please make self care a priority. When you feel that your own cup is filled, it becomes so much easier to show empathy and authenticity in forming positive relationships with your patients. If you think of empathy like having a limited pocket full of coins, and each day you spend the coins. Eventually there are no more coins to give and that means it’s time for you to take better care of yourself. This is a difficult and often thankless career, but you have idea the impact you make in the lives of others. Some will remember you for a lifetime. Live by your values, remember your why, and show compassion to yourself too.

Empathy is absolutely crucial as a healthcare provider, especially as a new one. It's all about understanding and connecting with your patients on a deeper level. When you show empathy, you're able to put yourself in their shoes and truly grasp their experiences, emotions, and concerns.

By being empathetic, you create a safe and supportive environment for your patients. It helps build trust and rapport, which is essential for effective healthcare. When patients feel heard, understood, and cared for, it can greatly enhance their overall experience and even contribute to better health outcomes.

Empathy allows you to provide personalized care that is tailored to each individual's unique needs. It helps you communicate effectively, not just through words, but also through non-verbal cues and active listening. This can make a world of difference in how patients perceive their treatment and how well they adhere to 

So, as a new healthcare provider, remember that empathy is not just a nice-to-have quality, but an essential one. It will not only benefit your patients but also contribute to your professional growth and satisfaction.

column64:
Hey there,

Congratulations on starting your journey as a healthcare provider! It's definitely a challenging but incredibly rewarding path. I'd be happy to share some insights based on my experiences.

One important aspect of providing healthcare is understanding and prioritizing patients' perspectives. When patients feel heard and valued, it can have a profound impact on their self-efficacy and belief in their ability to improve their health. For example, I remember a patient who was hesitant to follow a treatment plan due to concerns about side effects. By taking the time to listen and address their fears, we were able to find a solution that worked for them and fostered their confidence in managing their health.

Adopting a patient-centered approach is key in building trust. Making small changes in your practice, such as actively involving patients in their healthcare visits, can make a big difference. I've seen how taking the time to explain medical information in a way that patients can understand and involving them in decision-making can greatly enhance their trust in medical care. This, in turn, leads to better engagement and improved health outcomes.

Being sensitive to the circumstances that may impact a patient's journey towards better health is crucial. Understanding the challenges they may face, such as financial constraints or limited access to resources, allows us to work together to find practical solutions. By acknowledging and addressing these barriers, we empower patients to take an active role in their healthcare, increasing compliance and promoting long-term well-being.

Remember, each patient is unique, and it's important to approach their care with empathy and respect. By prioritizing their perspectives, aligning goals, and creating a supportive environment, you can make a positive impact on their health and overall experience.

Wishing you all the best in your new role!

Take care,
Maria H

One of the primary reasons I decided to pursue nursing is my innate desire to help people during their most vulnerable moments. The idea of being able to provide comfort, care, and support to individuals in need resonates deeply with me. Nursing offers a unique opportunity to directly contribute to the well-being of others, whether it's through administering medication, comforting patients, or advocating for their needs. Making a tangible difference in someone's life is incredibly rewarding and a constant motivation source.

Furthermore, my own experiences have played a significant role in shaping my decision to pursue nursing. Growing up, I witnessed firsthand the compassionate care provided by nurses to my family members during times of illness. Their dedication, empathy, and unwavering commitment left a lasting impression on me and instilled a sense of admiration for the nursing profession. These experiences ignited my passion to follow in their footsteps and become a source of comfort and support for others in similar situations.

Nursing offers diverse opportunities for growth, specialization, and professional development. From working in hospitals and clinics to community health settings and beyond, the field of nursing presents endless possibilities to explore and expand one's skill set. The prospect of continuously learning and adapting to new challenges excites me and reinforces my decision to pursue a career in nursing.
In conclusion, my decision to pursue a career in nursing is driven by a combination of personal passion, admiration for the profession, and a desire to make a meaningful difference in the lives of others. Inspired by the compassionate care provided by nurses and fueled by my own experiences, I am eager to embark on this rewarding journey and contribute to the health and well-being of individuals and communities alike.
